newsitem.title: UK: Norway crown dealt short-lived blow by resignation.
newsitem.headline: Norway crown dealt short-lived blow by resignation.

text.p: The Norwegian crown was hit on Wednesday following the sudden resignation of Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, which surprised currency markets in the midst of Norway's 1997 budget negotations.

"The prime minister has resigned -- the problem here is that the budget negotiations are under way and they are running into problems," said Keld Holm, Lehman Brothers international economist. "The timing is a bit odd," he added.
But strong oil prices, Norway's key source of revenue, and economic stability will ensure the move is short-lived, analysts and traders said.
"I think the reaction is a temporary, knee-jerk one," said a trader.

While the crown took a knock, it has been the strength of the mark -- which powered on Tuesday to a 3 1/2 year high of 74.05 against the yen -- that has been in the driving seat of European currencies.
"I think it's as much a mark story, because it is doing generally better," the trader added.
At 1205 GMT the Norwegian crown was trading at 4.2455/65 per mark against 4.2345/55 in late European trade on Tuesday.
Brundtland, 57, announced on Wednesday she would be stepping down on Friday and hand over power to Labour Party leader Thorbjoern Jagland.
While the unexpected timing of her resignation unsettled the crown in Europe, traders and analysts said the appointment of Jagland was also unnerving.
"He (Jagland) is seen as more closely related to the unions than the former prime minister was," said Holm.
Holm said Norway, one of the few European countries to enjoy a budget surplus, needed a strong prime minister who could say "no' to the unions.
"Clearly, Jagland has a reputation of being slightly less tough," he added.
According to the draft budget proposal for 1997, the surplus is expected to reach 37.9 billion crowns ($5.8 billion) in 1996 and rise to 40.9 billion crowns next year.
With the temptation to dip into government coffers to assuage the country's unions, analysts fear the inflationary ghost may appear.
"Norway is floating in money," said Holm.
